---
title: "Decision Guide and the Unified Table"
---

The book has derived some twenty methods, and every one of them turned out to be a choice along the
same few axes: where the training signal comes from, which samples the gradient uses, what weight each
sample gets, what keeps the update stable, at what granularity credit is assigned, and which target
the whole procedure is aiming at. This chapter turns that into two practical tools. The first is a
procedure for choosing a method given the signal and the budget you actually have, and for knowing
what to watch while it trains. The second is a way to place a *new* method on the map in a few
minutes, by asking the same questions of its paper. The unified table, assembled from the method
cards, is the reference for both.

## A procedure for choosing a method

Work through five questions in order. Each one narrows the families that fit.

**1. What signal do you have?**

| You have | The natural families | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| demonstrations of good behavior | SFT (behavior cloning); off-policy distillation if they come from a model | [LLM as a policy](04-the-llm-as-a-policy.qmd), [imitation](09-imitating-a-better-distribution.qmd) |
| pairwise preferences, already collected | DPO and its variants; or a reward model + RL | [direct preference](07-direct-preference-methods.qmd), [rewards](05-rewards.qmd) |
| a preference annotator you can query (human or model) | online DPO; reward model + on-policy RL | [direct preference](07-direct-preference-methods.qmd), [shared target](06-the-shared-target.qmd) |
| thumbs-up / thumbs-down on single responses | KTO; or filtering | [direct preference](07-direct-preference-methods.qmd) |
| a verifier (tests, answer checker) | critic-free policy gradients (RLOO, GRPO and its fixes); rejection-sampling fine-tuning | [critic-free](08-policy-gradients-without-a-critic.qmd), [imitation](09-imitating-a-better-distribution.qmd) |
| a stronger model whose log-probabilities you can query | on-policy distillation | [imitation](09-imitating-a-better-distribution.qmd) |
| outcomes against which a stated probability can be scored | correctness + a bounded proper scoring rule | [calibration](10-rewarding-calibration.qmd) |

**2. Can you sample from the current policy and score the samples during training?** If yes,
on-policy methods are available, and they are the ones that learn from the model's own mistakes (the
DAgger argument of the [LLM-as-policy chapter](04-the-llm-as-a-policy.qmd)) and that, on the toy
language, kept converging where offline methods drifted. If no, you are offline: DPO-family methods on
a fixed dataset, or one round of filtering. Expect the offline costs measured in the
[direct-preference chapter](07-direct-preference-methods.qmd): no exploration, overfitting the
dataset's deterministic preferences, and the policy drifting away from the data's distribution. A
middle path is iterated: collect, train, re-collect.

**3. What can you hold in memory?** PPO-based RLHF needs four models (policy, reference, reward model,
critic). Critic-free methods with a verifiable reward need two (policy, reference) or one if the KL
term is dropped. DPO needs two, and the reference's log-probabilities can be precomputed. SimPO and
ORPO need one. On-policy distillation needs the student and the teacher.

**4. What target do you want, and does your implementation actually aim at it?** If the goal is the
KL-regularized optimum $\pi^\star$, check how the KL is implemented: "$k_1$ in the reward" and "$k_2$ as a
loss" target it; "$k_3$ as a loss" regularizes the forward KL instead and lands elsewhere
([keeping updates stable](03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd)). Check what the advantage normalization does:
dividing by a group's standard deviation reweights prompts and weakens the KL relative to the reward,
and dividing by each response's length biases length
([critic-free](08-policy-gradients-without-a-critic.qmd)). If the method has no reference model at all
(SimPO, ORPO, DAPO), it has no $\pi^\star$; decide whether that matters for your use.

**5. What will you monitor?** Every failure mode in the book has a signature that can be watched.

| Watch | Because | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| KL from $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ | the axis along which overoptimization happens; a KL penalty mostly decides where on it training stops | [rewards](05-rewards.qmd) |
| reward on a held-out *true* metric, not just the training reward | a learned or hackable reward keeps rising after the true one peaks | [rewards](05-rewards.qmd) |
| response length (for correct and incorrect responses separately) | length bias from reward models and from per-response normalization | [rewards](05-rewards.qmd), [critic-free](08-policy-gradients-without-a-critic.qmd) |
| entropy, and the diversity of correct answers | collapse from unregularized optimization and iterated filtering | [imitation](09-imitating-a-better-distribution.qmd), [what RL does](11-what-rl-does-to-a-model.qmd) |
| fraction of groups with zero reward variance | the share of the batch that carries no signal | [critic-free](08-policy-gradients-without-a-critic.qmd) |
| fraction of tokens clipped | clipping silences tokens rather than flagging problems | [stable updates](03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd) |
| likelihood of the preferred responses (preference methods) | likelihood displacement | [direct preference](07-direct-preference-methods.qmd) |
| calibration of any stated confidence, per data slice | pooled calibration can hide per-slice base-rate errors | [calibration](10-rewarding-calibration.qmd) |

## Classical RL vs LLM-era RL, revisited

The [LLM-as-policy chapter](04-the-llm-as-a-policy.qmd) gave a table of what became of each classical
concept. Having derived the methods, three of its rows can be stated more sharply.

- **The critic** was dropped for single-turn reasoning because a group of samples gives an unbiased
  per-prompt baseline at the cost of extra generation, and the measured benefit of an exact per-token
  critic over a per-prompt baseline was small on the toy language
  ([policy gradients](02-policy-gradients.qmd)). It returns where consequences are delayed across turns
  ([what RL does](11-what-rl-does-to-a-model.qmd)).
- **The KL to a reference** is the one genuinely new structural element, and its implementation
  decides the target ([stable updates](03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd),
  [shared target](06-the-shared-target.qmd)).
- **Off-policy learning** survives mainly as offline preference optimization (DPO), which avoids
  importance sampling altogether by not sampling, and as mild staleness in asynchronous pipelines,
  corrected by ratios and clips.

## Placing a new paper on the map in five minutes

When a new post-training method appears, ask its paper the method-card questions, in this order. Most
papers answer each in a sentence, usually in the method section or the main equation.

1. **Signal.** What does the training signal say, and who produced it: demonstrations, preferences,
   binary labels, a learned reward, a verifier, a judge, a teacher's log-probabilities, a scored
   probability?
2. **Sampling distribution $q$.** Which responses does the gradient use: a fixed dataset, the current
   policy, an older policy, a teacher?
3. **Weight $w$.** Write the gradient as $\mathbb{E}_{q}[w\,\nabla\log\pi_\theta]$. What is $w$, per
   sample or per token? Can it be negative? Is it normalized, and by what?
4. **Stability.** What stops the policy moving too far: a KL (to what, in which direction, implemented
   how), a clip (on what ratio, at which granularity), nothing?
5. **Credit.** Is the weight per sequence, per step or per token?
6. **Target.** If everything were exact, which distribution would the procedure converge to? Is it
   $\pi^\star$ for some reward and $\beta$, or something else?

Then name the classical idea it reuses, and the method it modifies. That is a row of the unified
table.

**A worked example: Math-Shepherd.** The paper trains a process reward model whose label for each
reasoning step is the fraction of $N$ completions from that step that reach the correct answer, and
then "employ[s it] to reinforce LLMs with step-by-step Proximal Policy Optimization" [@wang2023mathshepherd].
*Signal*: a learned process reward, per step. *Sampling*: the current policy, as in PPO. *Weight*: PPO's
clipped advantage, now with rewards at every step instead of only at the end. *Stability*: PPO's clip
(and whatever KL the implementation uses, which the reader should check). *Credit*: step level, from a
reward that is a Monte Carlo estimate of the value of each partial solution. *Target*: the
KL-regularized optimum of the process-reward-shaped objective. *Classical lineage*: PPO with a learned
value function used as a shaping reward. *Parent*: PPO-based RLHF, with the outcome reward model replaced
by a process reward model. The [rewards chapter](05-rewards.qmd) predicts its risk: a learned value is a
proxy, and a policy optimized against it will find where it is wrong.

## The final test

The book set out to move a reader from

> "RLHF, DPO, and GRPO are three alignment techniques I've heard of."

to

> "All three target a KL-regularized reward objective whose optimum is the reference policy tilted by
> $\exp(r/\beta)$. RLHF learns a reward from preferences and climbs toward that optimum with an on-policy
> policy gradient, using a learned critic as baseline and a clip as trust region. DPO uses the closed
> form to cancel the reward model out and fits the policy to fixed preference pairs by logistic
> regression, giving up exploration. GRPO keeps the on-policy policy gradient but replaces the critic
> with a Monte Carlo baseline computed from a group of samples per prompt, which works well when rewards
> are verifiable."

with one amendment that the toy language forced: GRPO *as published*, with its KL estimator in the loss
and its standard-deviation normalization, regularizes a different divergence than RLHF and lands
somewhere else. And from

> "RL is a different kind of ML from supervised learning."

to

> "RL differs in where the data comes from and what the feedback says. Its gradient is a weighted
> maximum-likelihood gradient on samples the learner chose to generate. SFT is the special case of
> weight 1 on someone else's samples."
